hints: Focus on the word 'most' in the question. CO2 has three ways to travel, but one carries about 85% of it, so think about which form dominates.
Remember what happens inside the red blood cell when CO2 enters: carbonic anhydrase makes carbonic acid, which then splits to release the ion that moves out into the plasma.
walkthrough:
**Recall the three transport routes**

Think of CO2 leaving respiring tissues and entering red blood cells. It can travel dissolved, bound to haemoglobin, or converted to another ion.

Rough split to remember:
$$\text{hydrogencarbonate} \approx 85\% > \text{carbamino} \approx 10\% > \text{dissolved} \approx 5\%$$

**Follow the main chemical pathway**

Inside the red cell, the enzyme carbonic anhydrase speeds up this key reaction. This is the heart of CO2 transport.

$$CO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2CO_3 \rightarrow H^+ + HCO_3^-$$

**Pick the 'most' form**

The hydrogen ions are buffered by haemoglobin, while the hydrogencarbonate ions ($HCO_3^-$) diffuse out into the plasma for transport to the lungs. Since this route carries the vast majority, option C is the answer.

options.A: Carbaminohaemoglobin (CO2 bound directly to haemoglobin) is real but only carries about 10% of CO2, so not the most.
options.B: Carbonic acid (H2CO3) is only a very short-lived intermediate that quickly dissociates, so it is not a transport form.
options.C: Correct. About 85% of CO2 is carried as hydrogencarbonate ions (HCO3-) dissolved in the plasma after formation in red cells.
options.D: Only about 5% travels dissolved in solution in plasma and cytoplasm, far too little to be the main method.
